q: A dealer in Delhi sells goods to a buyer in Uttar Pradesh. Which tax applies?
exp: Inter-state supplies attract IGST, levied and collected by the Centre and later apportioned to the destination state.

q: A supplier in Chandigarh sells goods to a buyer in Chandigarh. Which taxes apply?
exp: Chandigarh is a Union Territory without a legislature, so intra-UT supplies attract CGST plus UTGST.

q: Which of these Union Territories levies SGST rather than UTGST?
exp: Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir have legislatures and are treated as 'States' for GST, so they levy SGST.

q: GST is a destination-based consumption tax.
exp: Tax revenue goes to the state where goods or services are consumed, which is why place of supply rules matter so much.

q: Under which Act is IGST on imported goods actually levied?
exp: The IGST Act says IGST on imports is levied under the Customs Tariff Act, collected at the border along with customs duty.

q: Which statement about IGST is correct?
options: It is shared only among states
It is collected by the Centre and apportioned between the Centre and the destination state
It is collected by the origin state
It is a cess over and above CGST
exp: IGST roughly equals CGST plus SGST; the Centre collects it and settles the state's share with the consuming state.

q: A company with branches in Maharashtra and Karnataka can use one GSTIN for both states.
exp: Registration is state-wise. A business needs a separate GSTIN in every state or UT from which it makes taxable supplies.

q: When did GST come into force in India?
exp: GST was rolled out on 1 July 2017.

q: Which Constitutional amendment enabled GST?
exp: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 introduced Articles 246A, 269A and 279A. (It was the 122nd Amendment Bill.)

q: Which Article of the Constitution establishes the GST Council?
exp: Article 279A creates the GST Council. 246A gives concurrent taxing power and 269A covers inter-state supplies.

q: Who chairs the GST Council?
options: A state finance minister chosen by rotation
exp: The Union Finance Minister chairs it; state finance ministers are members and the Union MoS Finance is also a member.

q: How are votes weighted in the GST Council?
options: Centre 1/3, all states together 2/3, with decisions needing a 3/4 majority
One vote per member, simple majority
Centre has a veto, states advise
exp: The Centre's vote carries one-third weight and the states together two-thirds. A decision needs at least three-fourths of the weighted votes, so neither side can push something through alone.

q: GST Council recommendations are directly binding law without any notification.
exp: The Council recommends. Changes take effect through Acts passed by Parliament and legislatures or notifications issued by governments. The Supreme Court in Mohit Minerals (2022) also called its recommendations persuasive rather than binding.

q: Which of these was NOT subsumed into GST?
exp: Basic customs duty continues on imports. Service tax, VAT and most central excise were subsumed.

q: Which of these taxes still exists alongside GST?
exp: Stamp duty, electricity duty, property tax and customs duty are outside GST. Entry tax, octroi and luxury tax were subsumed.

q: Entertainment tax levied by local bodies (panchayats, municipalities) was fully subsumed into GST.
exp: Entertainment tax levied by states was subsumed, but local bodies' power to tax entertainment survives under Entry 62 of List II.

q: Which item is outside GST under the Constitution itself?
exp: Alcohol for human consumption is excluded from the definition of goods and services tax in Article 366(12A). Petroleum products are within GST's scope but not taxed until the Council recommends a date.

q: Which of these is within GST law but GST is not currently levied on it?
exp: Crude oil, high speed diesel, petrol, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel are covered by section 9(2) CGST: GST applies only from a date notified on the Council's recommendation.

q: A company's only sales are petrol and diesel. Does it need GST registration for those sales?
options: No, persons dealing only in non-taxable supplies are not required to register
exp: Persons engaged exclusively in non-taxable or wholly exempt supplies aren't liable to register.

q: A restaurant sells both food and liquor. How is each taxed and what's the effect on its input tax credit?
model: Food service is taxed under GST. Liquor for human consumption is outside GST and attracts state VAT/excise instead. Because liquor sales are a non-taxable supply, common input tax credit has to be apportioned and the part attributable to liquor reversed.
points: Food under GST, liquor under state VAT
Common ITC is apportioned under section 17(2) and rule 42/43
exp: Non-taxable supplies count as exempt supplies for ITC apportionment.

q: After the GST rate rationalisation effective 22 September 2025, what are the two main rate slabs for most goods and services?
exp: The 12% and 28% slabs were largely folded in: most items moved to 5% or 18%, with a 40% rate for a short list of luxury and sin goods.

q: After September 2025, which rate applies to a narrow set of luxury and sin goods (like pan masala or large cars)?
exp: The 40% special rate replaced 28% plus compensation cess for most of these items. Some tobacco products kept cess until the compensation loans are repaid.

q: Which special low rate applies to gold and silver?
exp: Gold, silver and jewellery are taxed at 3%. Rough diamonds and precious stones have 0.25%.

q: GST compensation cess was introduced to compensate states for revenue loss during the transition to GST.
exp: The GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 guaranteed states 14% annual growth on base-year revenue for five years, funded by the cess. After 2022 it continued to repay loans taken to cover shortfalls.

q: Individual life and health insurance premiums after 22 September 2025 are:
exp: The Council exempted individual life and health insurance policies (including reinsurance of these) as part of the 2025 rationalisation.
